title: Krishna
tomorrow: one name in Vishnu's line surprises people. whose, and why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita's rhythm: whenever dharma slips, Krishna comes, yuge yuge, age after age. Today, the end of his time on earth, and the hunter who caused it.

A phone knocked into a pool. A borrowed car with a fresh dent. A friend who did real damage without meaning to and now can't stop saying sorry. The Bhagavata Purana tells one of these at the very end of Krishna's life. A hunter named Jara sees something move among the leaves near the sea, takes it for a deer, and lets an arrow fly. It isn't a deer. It's Krishna's foot. Jara runs up, sees whom he has hit, and falls at his feet, shaking. And the first thing Krishna says to him is: don't be afraid. Get up.
screen: `DAMAGE NOBODY MEANT.` → `AN ARROW FOR A DEER.` → `DON'T BE AFRAID. GET UP.`

segments.voice: The scene is already sorrowful before the arrow flies. Krishna's own clan, the Yadus, has torn itself apart in a drunken quarrel by the sea, and his brother Balarama has already left the world. Krishna sits quietly under a tree, one foot resting across his thigh. Then the arrow. Jara begs him: I did this without knowing. Punish me. Krishna's answer turns the whole scene. Don't be afraid, Jara. Get up. This happened by my own wish. And the text says Krishna sends the hunter on to heaven. Look at what he doesn't do. He doesn't make Jara earn it, or ask for a second apology, or a speech. The one who is wounded is the one who steadies the other. Forgiveness here begins with the frightened person's fear, before the injury is even talked about. Then Krishna leaves the world, and the Bhagavata adds a line that matters for these weeks: on the day he went, the age of Kali came in. So the gentlest scene of his story stands at the hinge between two ages, and the names still to come in Vishnu's line belong to the harder one.
screen: `A CLAN FALLS APART BY THE SEA.` · `AN ARROW, MEANT FOR A DEER.` · `DON'T BE AFRAID. GET UP.` · `THE AGE OF KALI COMES IN.` · then, large: `THE WOUNDED ONE STEADIES THE OTHER.`

segments.voice: With a pen and any scrap of paper, write one short line you could say to someone who hurt you without meaning to. Keep it as short as Krishna's was. Then set the pen down and breathe with the paper in front of you for the rest of the sit; nobody has to see it.
Krishna: wounded by a hunter's stray arrow at the end of his life, he told the hunter, don't be afraid, get up.
Your line: Krishna. The arrow came from a stranger, and the first word back was don't be afraid. Day fifteen fifty-nine, done.

notes: Krishna run, day 4 of 4 (1556–1559). Angle: his departure, read as forgiveness that starts with the frightened person. For parents: this is a death scene, told gently, with no crisis content; it is fine to pause on it with a child.

Details from Bhagavata 11.30: the Yadus' drunken quarrel at Prabhasa; Balarama leaving first; Krishna seated under a tree with his foot on his thigh; Jara mistakes the foot for a deer; Krishna says 'ma bhair jare, uttishtha', it was his own wish, and sends Jara to heaven. Krishna then speaks to his charioteer Daruka, so the script avoids calling Jara the last person he speaks to. Confirm each.
Original 'मा भैः' (ma bhaih) is the form behind 'ma bhair' in the verse; confirm spelling.
'On the day Krishna went back, the age of Kali came in' paraphrases Bhagavata 12.2 (around verses 29–33). Confirm the verse.
